correctness.rationale: The shortest chord types give two strictly opposing monotone functions; their crossing yields the packing height. All facets are two polar caps and 2n lateral triangles, whose exact distances from the origin yield the covering cosine profile. Differentiating the side-facet distance squared proves a unique crossing/maximum and the 2/(2n+2)/2n facet-normal phase. The analytic comparison simplifies to a positive factor for n>=4; the n->infinity limits follow from cosine expansion. A standalone checker independently enumerates facets and pairwise chords and passes 2412 numerical checks, which are supporting rather than sufficient for universal proof.

evidence: Fowler et al. (2002) seek global antipodally constrained cap arrangements for finitely many point counts; their ten-point optimum is not an antiprism. A theorem on globally optimal configurations for a fixed finite count does not imply the complete all-n constrained one-parameter profile.

Wimmer (2017), DOI 10.1007/s00454-017-9891-x, reports unconstrained globally optimal eight-cap geometry. Only a publisher preview was accessible; direct full-text coverage cannot be ruled out for n=4, but no every-n theorem was established from the available material.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The global finite-N results are mathematically different quantified problems. Even if their optimal configurations have better covering radii than this restricted class, that does not imply the restricted-class optimum at each n or the phase diagram.

value.rationale: Sphere packing and covering compete within the same natural finite symmetric family. The exact all-n cover height and farthest-hole contact-count transition explain why the uniquely densest equal-edge antiprism loses an asymptotic 45 degrees of covering radius: a structural discrepancy, not an arbitrary finite-parameter computation. The family is directly motivated by established packing-to-covering sphere literature and gives a benchmark for designing staggered-ring cap constellations.
